title: 26 U.S. Code Section 41(b)(3) Contract Research Expenses
description: Under 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(3), 65% of contract research payments count (75% for consortia, 100% for energy research) if the agreement precedes the work.
summary: Under 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(3), U.S. taxpayers claiming the federal R&D tax credit may count 65 percent of payments to non-employee contractors for qualified research as contract research expenses, 75 percent for qualified research consortia, and 100 percent for eligible energy research, provided the agreement precedes the research, grants rights to results, and leaves the taxpayer bearing failure risk.

body.text: Under 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(3), U.S. taxpayers claiming the federal R&D tax credit may count 65 percent of payments to non-employee contractors for qualified research as contract research expenses, 75 percent for qualified research consortia, and 100 percent for eligible energy research, provided the agreement precedes the research, grants rights to results, and leaves the taxpayer bearing failure risk.

Under 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(3)(A), "contract research expenses" are defined as 65 percent of any amount paid or incurred by a taxpayer to any person—other than an employee of the taxpayer—for qualified research. Enacted as a core pillar of the Credit for Increasing Research Activities under Internal Revenue Code (IRC) Section 41, this statutory limitation permits businesses to include outsourced research and development (R&D) expenditures in their federal credit calculation base while applying a mandatory 35 percent statutory reduction ("haircut") designed to strip out the third-party contractor's commercial profit margin, general and administrative overhead, and non-qualifying indirect expenses. Depending on the statutory classification of the counterparty and the scientific nature of the underlying work, IRC Section 41(b)(3) elevates this statutory inclusion rate to 75 percent for payments made to qualified scientific research consortia (26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(3)(C)) and to 100 percent for payments made to eligible small businesses, universities, or federal laboratories conducting qualified energy research (26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(3)(D)).

Capturing contract research expenses under IRC Section 41(b)(3) requires satisfying a rigorous matrix of statutory, regulatory, and judicial requirements governing agreement timing, financial risk allocation, intellectual property rights, and domestic performance. Under Treasury Regulation § 1.41-2(e) and the "funded research" exclusion of 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(4)(H) and Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4A(d), an outsourced research expenditure qualifies for the payer only if the agreement is entered into prior to the performance of the qualified research, the research is performed on behalf of the taxpayer (requiring the taxpayer to hold a right to the research results), and the taxpayer bears the financial risk of technical failure. Furthermore, following the July 2025 enactment of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA, P.L. 119-21), which added IRC Section 174A, domestic contract research expenditures once again qualify for permanent immediate deductibility for taxable years beginning after December 31, 2024, whereas foreign contract research remains completely excluded from the Section 41 credit under 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(4)(F) and subject to mandatory 15-year amortization under IRC Section 174.
1. Legislative History and Economic Rationale of the Contract Research Provision
Enactment Under ERTA 1981 and the Spillover Justification

Congress first established the federal research and experimentation (R&E) tax credit—including the contract research expense provision—in the Economic Recovery Tax Act of 1981 (ERTA, P.L. 97-34), enacted on August 13, 1981 (originally codified at IRC Section 44F before its subsequent redesignation as IRC Section 41). As documented in the Joint Committee on Taxation's General Explanation of the Economic Recovery Tax Act of 1981 (JCS-71-81, published December 1981), Congress enacted the credit to reverse a troubling macroeconomic decline in domestic R&D investment that had eroded United States productivity growth, industrial capacity, and international market competitiveness. The initial credit applied to qualified expenditures incurred from July 1, 1981, through December 31, 1985, and was intentionally structured as an incremental subsidy to reward research spending above a historical base period rather than subsidizing baseline research that businesses would have undertaken regardless of tax policy.

The economic foundation of IRC Section 41 rests on correcting a classic market failure: the divergence between the private rate of return and the social rate of return on R&D investment caused by positive "spillover effects" (also termed "neighborhood effects"). When a private enterprise invests capital in technological experimentation, the resulting scientific knowledge, engineering methodologies, and trained technical workforce inevitably diffuse across the broader economy through competitor adoption, reverse engineering, academic publication, workforce mobility, and eventual patent expiration. Because the innovating firm cannot fully internalize or capture the aggregate societal benefits of its discoveries, private capital markets systematically underinvest in risky research relative to the socially optimal level. By reducing the after-tax marginal cost of R&D, IRC Section 41 lowers the financial hurdle rate for high-risk technological ventures and aligns private investment incentives closer to the social optimum.
Empirical Evaluations by the GAO and Permanent Codification

Federal oversight agencies have repeatedly evaluated both the economic efficacy and the administrative friction of the research tax credit. In its 1989 empirical study of the credit's initial implementation period (1981–1985), the General Accounting Office (now the Government Accountability Office, GAO) concluded that the credit raised corporate R&D investment above baseline econometric projections, stimulating between $1 billion and $2.5 billion in additional qualified research spending between 1981 and 1985. In a subsequent comprehensive 2009 report (GAO-10-136, Tax Policy: The Research Tax Credit's Design and Administration Can Be Improved, published November 2009), the GAO estimated that in tax year 2005 the credit reduced the after-tax price of additional qualified research by 6.4 percent to 7.3 percent on average. However, GAO-10-136 also highlighted sharp disparities in marginal incentive rates across taxpayers (ranging from 0 percent to 13 percent), substantial "windfall" credits attributable to outdated 1980s base-period formulas, and costly compliance controversies between taxpayers and the IRS over substantiating qualified expenditures.

Following its initial 1981 enactment, the federal research credit was temporarily extended 16 times and substantially modified 5 times—most notably in the Tax Reform Act of 1986 (P.L. 99-514), which reduced the regular credit rate from 25 percent to 20 percent and narrowed the statutory definition of qualified research to focus on technological uncertainty and experimentation. After more than three decades of temporary expirations and retroactive legislative renewals that impeded long-term corporate R&D budgeting, Congress permanently codified IRC Section 41 in the Protecting Americans from Tax Hikes (PATH) Act of 2015 (P.L. 114-113).
Analysis of the 65 Percent Statutory Proxy

Modern industrial R&D frequently spans outside engineering consultancies, specialized testing laboratories, contract research organizations (CROs) in the pharmaceutical and biotechnology sectors, and independent software developers. When Congress established the 65 percent inclusion rule under IRC Section 41(b)(3)(A), it sought to balance competitive neutrality between in-house and outsourced innovation against the fiscal risk of subsidizing non-research commercial costs.

While in-house Qualified Research Expenses (QREs) under 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(2) are strictly limited to direct employee wages for qualified services, direct tangible supplies consumed in research, and eligible off-premises computer leasing costs, a third-party contractor's fee bundles direct research labor and supplies together with the vendor's commercial profit margin, general and administrative overhead, facilities costs, and equipment depreciation. Rather than forcing taxpayers and IRS examiners to audit the internal cost accounting ledgers of unrelated third-party vendors on every invoice, Congress enacted the 65 percent statutory ceiling as an administrative proxy for the underlying direct wages and supplies embedded within a third-party contract fee. As illustrated in Treasury Regulation § 1.41-2(e)(5), Example 3, even when a contractor's itemized invoice explicitly breaks down $90x of labor, $20x of supplies, $50x of equipment depreciation, $40x of overhead ($200x total cost), and $100x of profit ($300x total payment), the paying taxpayer does not strip out the contractor's depreciation or overhead line by line; instead, the taxpayer simply applies the flat 65 percent statutory rate to the entire $300x non-contingent payment to arrive at $195x of contract research QREs.
2. Statutory and Regulatory Mechanics of 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(3)
Bifurcation of Qualified Research Expenses and the Three Statutory Inclusion Tiers

Under 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(1), a taxpayer's total QREs paid or incurred during the taxable year in carrying on any trade or business of the taxpayer (within the meaning of IRC Section 162) consist of the sum of (A) in-house research expenses and (B) contract research expenses. Notably, while 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(4) disregards the active trade or business requirement for in-house research expenses of startup ventures whose principal purpose is to use the research results in the active conduct of a future trade or business, Treasury Regulation § 1.41-2(a)(1)–(2) underscores that contract research expenses do not qualify under the startup exception and must be paid or incurred in carrying on an existing trade or business. Whereas eligible in-house wages, supplies, and off-premises computer usage costs are included in the QRE base at 100 percent of the qualified expenditure under 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(2), contract research expenditures are governed by a three-tier statutory percentage structure under 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(3).

In the actual text of the Internal Revenue Code, 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(3)(D) is titled "Amounts paid to eligible small businesses, universities, and Federal laboratories" and substitutes 100 percent for 65 percent when a taxpayer pays an eligible small business, an institution of higher education, or a Federal laboratory for qualified research that is energy research. Conversely, payments made to an "energy research consortium" for energy research are governed by a separate standalone sub-credit under 26 U.S.C. § 41(a)(3) (and defined in § 41(f)(6)), which provides a direct 20 percent tax credit on 100 percent of such payments rather than routing them through the incremental QRE base of Section 41(b)(3).

body.text: The Three-Part Regulatory Test Under Treasury Regulation § 1.41-2(e)

To qualify as a contract research expense under 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(3), an expenditure must satisfy the strict operational rules of 26 CFR § 1.41-2(e). Under Treasury Regulation § 1.41-2(e)(1), eligible payments encompass amounts paid or incurred in carrying on a trade or business to any person other than an employee for the performance on behalf of the taxpayer of either (i) qualified research as defined in § 1.41-4 or § 1.41-4A, or (ii) services which, if performed by employees of the taxpayer, would constitute "qualified services" within the meaning of IRC § 41(b)(2)(B) (engaging in, directly supervising, or directly supporting qualified research). Where a third-party contract calls for both qualified research/services and non-qualified services, only 65 percent of the specific portion attributable to qualified research or qualified services is eligible. Furthermore, as the IRS Audit Techniques Guide: Credit for Increasing Research Activities (i.e. Research Tax Credit) IRC § 41 - Qualified Research Expenses (updated July 2, 2026) explains, examiners distinguish between a general "service contract" (where a vendor is paid by the hour and the research is not specified, requiring examiners to verify the actual qualified work performed) and a "research contract" (where there is an agreed amount to perform specified qualified research).

Under Treasury Regulation § 1.41-2(e)(2), an expense is paid or incurred for the performance of qualified research only to the extent that it is paid or incurred pursuant to an agreement that satisfies three cumulative conditions:

items: Prior Agreement Requirement (26 CFR § 1.41-2(e)(2)(i)): The agreement must be "entered into prior to the performance of the qualified research". This requirement prevents taxpayers from retroactively characterizing the acquisition of an already-completed engineering study, clinical dataset, or off-the-shelf technology as commissioned contract research.

"On Behalf of the Taxpayer" Requirement (26 CFR § 1.41-2(e)(2)(ii) & (e)(3)): The agreement must provide that the research be performed "on behalf of the taxpayer". Under Treasury Regulation § 1.41-2(e)(3), qualified research is performed on behalf of the taxpayer "if the taxpayer has a right to the research results. Qualified research can be performed on behalf of the taxpayer notwithstanding the fact that the taxpayer does not have exclusive rights to the results". Additionally, under Treasury Regulation § 1.41-2(a)(1), a contract research expense is disqualified if the product or result of the research is intended to be transferred to another party in return for license or royalty payments and the taxpayer does not use the product of the research in its own trade or business.

Financial Risk / Non-Contingent Payment Requirement (26 CFR § 1.41-2(e)(2)(iii)): The agreement must require the taxpayer "to bear the expense even if the research is not successful". As Treasury Regulation § 1.41-2(e)(2) states: "If an expense is paid or incurred pursuant to an agreement under which payment is contingent on the success of the research, then the expense is considered paid for the product or result rather than the performance of the research, and the payment is not a contract research expense. The previous sentence applies only to that portion of a payment which is contingent on the success of the research". As illustrated in Treasury Regulation § 1.41-2(e)(5), Example 4, if a taxpayer agrees to reimburse a contractor for $200x of actual research expenses regardless of outcome and agrees to pay an additional $100x bonus only if the research is successful, only the non-contingent $200x qualifies for the 65 percent inclusion ($130x QRE), while the contingent $100x success fee is excluded ($0 QRE).

body.text: Verification against the verbatim text of 26 CFR § 1.41-2(e)(2) confirms that the regulation requires only "an agreement that—(i) Is entered into prior to the performance of the qualified research" and does not contain the word "written". Furthermore, the official IRS Audit Techniques Guide: Credit for Increasing Research Activities (i.e. Research Tax Credit) IRC § 41 - Qualified Research Expenses explicitly instructs IRS examiners that an expense qualifies if made pursuant to an agreement that is "usually in writing, but not required"—stating directly: "While the agreement is usually in writing, a written contract is not strictly required". From an audit defense standpoint, however, taxpayers should always execute formal written master services agreements (MSAs) and statements of work (SOWs) prior to performance, because proving prior agreement timing, financial risk allocation, and intellectual property rights without contemporaneous written documentation is exceptionally difficult under IRS examination.
Timing of Prepaid Contract Research Expenses

Under 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(3)(B) and Treasury Regulation § 1.41-2(e)(4), if any contract research expense paid or incurred during any taxable year is attributable to qualified research to be conducted after the close of that taxable year, the expense is treated for purposes of Section 41(b)(1)(B) as paid or incurred during the period in which the qualified research is actually conducted. As illustrated in Treasury Regulation § 1.41-2(e)(5), Example 2, if a calendar-year cash-method taxpayer pays a contractor $300x in Year 1 ($195x at 65 percent), but the contractor performs 50 percent of the research in Year 1 and 50 percent in Year 2, the taxpayer may claim only $97.5x (50 percent of $195x) as a contract research expense in Year 1 and must defer the remaining $97.5x to Year 2 when the research services are actually rendered. This statutory anti-acceleration rule prevents cash- or accrual-method taxpayers from artificially inflating current-year R&D tax credits by prepaying third-party contractor invoices prior to year-end.
3. The Four-Part Test and the Funded Research "Mirror Image" Doctrine
The Four-Part Test Under 26 U.S.C. § 41(d) and Regulatory Evolution

Whether performed in-house by employees or outsourced to an external contractor under Section 41(b)(3), the underlying research activity must satisfy the four-part statutory definition of "qualified research" set forth in 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(1) and Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4:

items: Section 174 / Section 174A Eligibility Test (26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(1)(A)): The activity must be research with respect to which expenditures may be treated as specified research or experimental expenditures under IRC Section 174 (or domestic research or experimental expenditures under IRC Section 174A for taxable years beginning after December 31, 2024), meaning costs incurred in an experimental or laboratory sense intended to eliminate uncertainty concerning the development or improvement of a product or process.

Technological in Nature Test (26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(1)(B)(i)): The research must be undertaken for the purpose of discovering information that is technological in nature, meaning the process of experimentation fundamentally relies on principles of the physical or biological sciences, engineering, or computer science.

Business Component / Permitted Purpose Test (26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(1)(B)(ii) & § 41(d)(2)–(3)): The application of the discovered information must be intended to be useful in the development of a new or improved business component of the taxpayer (any product, process, computer software, technique, formula, or invention to be held for sale, lease, or license, or used by the taxpayer in its trade or business) for a qualified purpose—specifically, a new or improved function, performance, reliability, or quality (expressly excluding style, taste, cosmetic, or seasonal design factors).

Process of Experimentation Test (26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(1)(C)): Substantially all—defined in Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4(a)(6) as 80 percent or more measured on a cost or other consistently applied reasonable basis—of the research activities for each business component must constitute elements of a process of experimentation for a qualified purpose.

body.text: Evolution of the "Discovery Test" (T.D. 8930 vs. T.D. 9104): Following the Tax Reform Act of 1986, intense controversy arose over the statutory phrase "undertaken for the purpose of discovering information" in 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(1)(B). On January 3, 2001, the Treasury Department and the IRS published final regulations in Treasury Decision (T.D.) 8930 (66 FR 280), which imposed a highly restrictive "discovery test" requiring that qualified research be undertaken to obtain knowledge that "exceeds, expands, or refines the common knowledge of skilled professionals in a particular field of science or engineering," alongside a rigid contemporaneous documentation requirement. Following widespread objections from taxpayers, industry coalitions, and members of Congress that T.D. 8930 contravened legislative history by requiring an extraordinary scientific breakthrough, Treasury and the IRS announced a comprehensive review in Notice 2001-19 (2001-10 I.R.B. 784, January 31, 2001), issued proposed regulations removing the discovery test in REG-112991-01 (66 FR 66362, December 26, 2001), and promulgated final regulations in T.D. 9104 (69 FR 22, published January 2, 2004, applicable to taxable years ending on or after December 31, 2003).

T.D. 9104 permanently eliminated both the T.D. 8930 "common knowledge of skilled professionals" discovery test and the separate contemporaneous documentation requirement (as well as removing subjective references to whether a design was "readily discernible and applicable" at the outset). Under Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4(a)(3) and § 1.41-4(a)(5)(i) (as finalized by T.D. 9104), research is undertaken for the purpose of discovering information whenever it is intended to eliminate uncertainty concerning the capability or method for developing or improving a business component, or the appropriate design of that business component. A process of experimentation is defined as "a process designed to evaluate one or more alternatives to achieve a result where the capability or the method of achieving that result, or the appropriate design of that result, is uncertain as of the beginning of the taxpayer's research activities". To satisfy this standard, the taxpayer (or its contractor) must: (1) identify the technical uncertainty regarding the development or improvement of the business component, (2) identify one or more alternatives intended to eliminate that uncertainty, and (3) identify and conduct a process of evaluating those alternatives (such as through modeling, simulation, or a systematic trial-and-error methodology).
The Funded Research Exclusion (IRC § 41(d)(4)(H)) and the Mirror Image Rule

The eligibility of a client to claim 65 percent of contract research expenses under 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(3) is the structural counterpart to the "funded research" exclusion under 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(4)(H), Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4(c)(9), and Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4A(d), which bars a researcher from claiming the credit for "any research to the extent funded by any grant, contract, or otherwise by another person (or governmental entity)". Together, Treasury Regulation § 1.41-2(e) (governing the paying client) and Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4A(d) (governing the performing contractor) coordinate credit eligibility to prevent two parties from "double dipping" on the same outsourced research activity. Under Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4A(d)(1), all agreements (not only formal research contracts) entered into between the performing researcher and other persons are examined on an expenditure-by-expenditure basis to determine the extent to which the research is funded.
Primary regulatory inspection of 26 CFR § 1.41-4A(d) establishes two critical legal nuances that break a strict binary outcome.

First, under Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4A(d)(2) (the "Neither Party Qualifies" Trap), if a contractor performing research for another person retains no substantial rights in the research (for example, the contract confers exclusive exploitation rights on the client and prohibits the contractor from using the research results in its own business without paying royalties), the research is treated as fully funded as to the contractor under Treasury Regulation § 1.41-2(a)(3)(i) and § 1.41-4A(d)(2), disqualifying the contractor from claiming any QREs. Simultaneously, if the client's payments to the contractor are contingent upon the success of the research, the client is barred from claiming contract research expenses under Treasury Regulation § 1.41-2(e)(2)(iii) because the payment is treated as an acquisition of a finished product or result rather than the performance of research. As Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4A(d)(2) explicitly codifies: "If a taxpayer performing research for another person retains no substantial rights in the research and if the payments to the researcher are contingent upon the success of the research, neither the performer nor the person paying for the research is entitled to treat any portion of the expenditures as qualified research expenditures".

Second, under Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4A(d)(3) and (d)(5) (Partial Funding and Pro-Rata Allocation), if a contractor retains substantial rights in the research (meaning it does not have to pay the client for the right to use the research results, beyond mere incidental benefits such as increased experience in a field of research) and receives non-contingent funding that is less than the contractor's total research expenses on the project, the research is treated as funded only to the extent of the payments (and fair market value of property) received. Under Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4A(d)(3)(i)–(ii), the contractor may claim its excess in-house QREs above the funded amount and, if its otherwise qualified research expenses exceed 65 percent of the funding, may establish a reasonable pro-rata allocation of the funding between qualified and non-qualified expenses (provided at least 65 percent of the funding is applied against otherwise qualified expenses). Finally, under Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4A(d)(5), if the extent of funding cannot be determined at the time the tax return is filed, the researcher must initially treat the research as completely funded and subsequently file an amended return once the funding amount is finally determined.
4. Federal Judicial Interpretation of Contract Research and Funded Research

Because neither IRC Section 41 nor Treasury Regulations treat a generic contract label (such as "fixed-price" or "time-and-materials") as automatically determinative, federal courts scrutinize the specific terms, invoicing milestones, acceptance testing protocols, termination-for-default provisions, warranty clauses, and intellectual property rights of each agreement.
Landmark Federal Circuit Precedents: Fairchild Industries and Lockheed Martin

In Fairchild Industries, Inc. v. United States, 71 F.3d 868 (Fed. Cir. 1995) (modified Feb. 23, 1996), rev'g 30 Fed. Cl. 839 (1994), Fairchild entered into a fixed-price incentive contract with the United States Air Force to design, develop, and build the T-46A Next Generation Trainer aircraft. The contract incorporated over 1,000 pages of technical specifications and required Fairchild to succeed at each design and testing milestone before the Air Force was obligated to accept and pay for the work on a line-item basis under the Defense Acquisition Regulations. Although Fairchild received bimonthly progress payments calculated as a percentage of incurred expenditures, those advances were fully refundable to the federal government if Fairchild defaulted or failed to deliver an aircraft meeting contract specifications. Reversing the Court of Federal Claims (which had erroneously focused on the practical likelihood of payment), the Federal Circuit held that the funded research inquiry turns on "who bears the research costs upon failure, not on whether the researcher is likely to succeed in performing the project". Because the Air Force was liable for payment only when the research succeeded and was formally accepted, Fairchild bore the financial risk of failure; consequently, the research was not funded, and Fairchild was entitled to claim its internal QREs.

In Lockheed Martin Corp. v. United States, 210 F.3d 1366 (Fed. Cir. 2000), rev'g in part 42 Fed. Cl. 485 (1998), Lockheed Martin (as successor to Martin Marietta) performed research under fixed-price federal government contracts that granted the United States government unlimited rights in technical data and a non-exclusive, paid-up license to use subject inventions, while also imposing statutory export restrictions (ITAR) and government cost-recoupment clauses on subsequent commercial sales. The Court of Federal Claims ruled that Lockheed lacked "substantial rights" under Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4A(d)(2) by analogizing to patent law's "all substantial rights" assignment doctrine. The Federal Circuit reversed, holding that patent assignment rules do not govern IRC Section 41 and establishing the controlling principle that "[t]he right to use the research results, even without the exclusive right, is a substantial right". Because Lockheed retained the legal right to use the developed technology in its own commercial business without paying royalties to the government for that right (with the court holding that statutory cost-recoupment clauses functioned as cost-recovery mechanisms rather than royalty payments), Lockheed retained substantial rights.
Capped Cost-Plus vs. Fixed-Price Contracts: Geosyntec and Populous Holdings

In Geosyntec Consultants, Inc. v. United States, 776 F.3d 1330 (11th Cir. 2015), Geosyntec, a specialty environmental and engineering consulting firm, sought a $1,677,432 federal research credit refund for tax years 2002 through 2005 across hundreds of client contracts. To litigate the funded research exclusion, the parties selected six representative contracts: three fixed-price contracts and three capped cost-plus contracts (under which Geosyntec was reimbursed for labor and expenses plus a markup, up to a contractual maximum ceiling price).

In reality, the district court held that Geosyntec's three fixed-price contracts were not funded (qualifying Geosyntec for a settled refund of $255,575 plus statutory interest on those fixed-price engagements), whereas the three capped cost-plus (cost-reimbursement subject to a ceiling) contracts were funded. On appeal of two capped cost-plus contracts (the Cherry Island Landfill contract and the Waste Management groundwater remediation contract), the Eleventh Circuit affirmed summary judgment for the United States, holding that budget-overrun risk under a ceiling cap ("cost-of-performance risk") is legally distinct from the financial risk of research failure required by Treasury Regulation § 1.41-2(e) and § 1.41-4A(d). Because Geosyntec billed and was paid monthly for predefined tasks and adherence to a general professional standard of care ("proper performance") rather than payment being conditioned on achieving a successful technical result ("successful performance"), the capped cost-plus contracts were funded by Geosyntec's clients—precluding Geosyntec from claiming the credit and shifting potential 65 percent contract research eligibility to the paying clients.

In Populous Holdings, Inc. v. Commissioner, U.S. Tax Court Docket No. 405-17 (Order dated December 6, 2019; Stipulated Decision entered January 16, 2020), Populous, an architectural design services firm, claimed research tax credits for tax years 2010 ($151,494 general business credit carryforward) and 2011 ($132,539 credit) across more than 100 contracts and subcontracts. Examining five representative fixed-price contracts (McEnery, Houston Dynamo, University of Arkansas, University of South Florida, and Pico Hall, three of which also included capped reimbursements for non-research travel and printing expenses), U.S. Tax Court Judge Joseph Robert Goeke granted summary judgment to Populous. On financial risk, the Tax Court held that none of the contracts paid Populous simply for performing research; rather, Populous was paid a fixed price for a final work product that required research, clients retained the right to review and approve design documents at each phase and dispute invoices, and Populous was contractually obligated to remedy any failed research or revise defective designs at its own expense without additional compensation. On substantial rights, the IRS argued that Populous lacked substantial rights in the McEnery, Pico Hall, and Houston Dynamo contracts because the clients owned the physical construction documents, models, renderings, and architectural copyrights. Rejecting the IRS's position, the Tax Court held that client ownership of physical documents and architectural copyrights does not strip the researcher of the non-exclusive right to use the underlying researched technology and engineering know-how in future projects without paying the clients.
Substantiation of Experimentation and Direct Supplies: Davenport and Union Carbide

In United States v. Davenport, 897 F. Supp. 2d 496 (N.D. Tex. 2012), Morris and David Davenport, equal 50 percent shareholders of Burly Corporation (whose subsidiary Mueller Supply Company Inc. manufactured residential metal roofing and stand-alone metal buildings), filed amended returns for tax years 2002 and 2003 claiming Section 41 credits for the "OneWorld Project". The project involved implementing and integrating a commercial J.D. Edwards OneWorld enterprise resource planning (ERP) software suite with an IBM ERP Bridge data collection package. Based on a study by alliantgroup L.P., the taxpayers claimed both in-house wages paid to Mueller employees and contract research expenses paid to four specific outside contractors (Steve Wilburn, Tracy Leaks, Ronald Hartin, and Shannon Bailey), while excluding fees paid to IBM and J.D. Edwards consultants.

Verification of the court's opinion in 897 F. Supp. 2d 496 establishes that while the taxpayers in Davenport did segregate employee wages from the four outside contractors in their refund filing, the Northern District of Texas did not adjudicate the 100 percent versus 65 percent arithmetic; instead, the court granted summary judgment to the United States (dismissing the 2002 claims with prejudice and ordering recovery of the erroneous 2003 refunds totaling $112,399 and $112,398 plus interest) and disallowed 100 percent of both the in-house employee wages and the outside contract research expenses. The court held that neither Mueller's employees nor the contractors engaged in a scientific "process of experimentation" under 26 U.S.C. § 41(d), as their activities consisted of routine software configuration, script testing, and requesting code modifications from IBM where the technical capability and method were already known at the outset. Davenport thus establishes the foundational audit rule that if an underlying software or engineering project fails the Section 41(d) process of experimentation test, neither internal employee wages nor third-party contractor fees can be claimed as QREs.

Finally, in Union Carbide Corp. & Subsidiaries v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2009-50, aff'd, 697 F.3d 104 (2d Cir. 2012), Union Carbide conducted plant-scale experimental runs on commercial chemical manufacturing processes (including its anticoking and UCAT-J projects) and claimed QREs for the full cost of raw materials consumed during those production test runs, even though the resulting finished chemicals were produced for commercial sale and sold to customers. Affirming the Tax Court, the Second Circuit deferred to Treasury Regulation § 1.41-2(b)(1) (which excludes "indirect research expenditures") and held that raw material supplies that would have been purchased for ordinary commercial production regardless of whether qualified research was being conducted do not qualify as supplies used in the conduct of qualified research under IRC Section 41(b)(2)(A)(ii).

body.text: 5. Intersection with IRC Section 174 and Section 174A: Capitalization vs. Immediate Expensing

Under 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(1)(A), a threshold prerequisite for any expenditure—including a third-party contract research expense under Section 41(b)(3)—to qualify for the Section 41 research credit is that the underlying research must be research with respect to which expenditures may be treated as specified research or experimental (SRE) expenditures under IRC Section 174 (or domestic research or experimental expenditures under IRC Section 174A). Over the past decade, the tax accounting rules governing Section 174 have undergone two major legislative transformations that directly dictate the after-tax cash-flow economics of domestic versus foreign contract research.
The TCJA Capitalization Mandate (Tax Years 2022–2024) and Procedural Guidance

From its original codification in the Internal Revenue Code of 1954 through December 31, 2021, former IRC Section 174(a)(1) permitted taxpayers to immediately deduct R&E expenditures in the taxable year paid or incurred. However, Section 13206(a) of the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act (TCJA) of 2017 (P.L. 115-97) amended IRC Section 174 for taxable years beginning after December 31, 2021, eliminating immediate expensing and requiring taxpayers to charge SRE expenditures (explicitly including software development costs under § 174(c)(3) and third-party contract research costs) to a capital account and amortize them ratably. Under this regime, domestic research was amortized ratably over 5 years beginning with the midpoint of the taxable year in which the expenses were paid or incurred, limiting the first-year deduction to 10 percent of the domestic expenditure ((1 / 5) × 0.5 = 10.00%). Foreign research—defined by reference to IRC § 41(d)(4)(F) as any research conducted outside the United States, the Commonwealth of Puerto Rico, or any possession of the United States—was amortized ratably over 15 years using the midpoint convention, yielding a first-year deduction of only 3.33 percent ((1 / 15) × 0.5 = 3.3333%).

To administer this mandatory accounting method change on a cut-off basis for the first taxable year beginning after December 31, 2021, the Treasury Department and the IRS issued Revenue Procedure 2023-8 (2023-3 I.R.B. 407, issued December 12, 2022) and subsequently Revenue Procedure 2023-11 (2023-3 I.R.B. 417, issued December 29, 2022, which modified and superseded Rev. Proc. 2023-8). These procedures waived the requirement to file a formal Form 3115 (Application for Change in Accounting Method) for a taxpayer's first taxable year beginning after December 31, 2021, authorizing taxpayers instead to attach a streamlined statement in lieu of Form 3115 citing Designated Automatic Accounting Method Change Number "265" (or to comply under a transition rule by properly reporting SRE amortization on Part VI of Form 4562, Depreciation and Amortization).
The One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA, July 2025) and IRC Section 174A

In July 2025, Congress enacted the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA, P.L. 119-21), which fundamentally bifurcated the federal tax accounting treatment of domestic and foreign contract research for taxable years beginning after December 31, 2024. Section 70302 of the OBBBA added IRC Section 174A, which restored permanent immediate deductibility (100 percent Year 1 deduction) for domestic research and experimental expenditures under Section 174A(a) in taxable years beginning after December 31, 2024. Alternatively, under Section 174A(c), taxpayers may elect to charge domestic R&E expenditures to a capital account and amortize them ratably over a period of not less than 60 months beginning with the month in which the taxpayer first realizes benefits from such expenditures. Furthermore, under Section 70302(f) of P.L. 119-21 and Section 7.02(2)(f) of Revenue Procedure 2025-28, taxpayers holding remaining unamortized domestic SRE balances incurred in taxable years beginning after December 31, 2021, and before January 1, 2025, may elect (via a statement in lieu of Form 3115 reported on Line 43 of Form 4562) to accelerate and deduct those remaining unamortized domestic balances either in full in the first taxable year beginning after December 31, 2024, or ratably over a two-taxable-year period.

As detailed in the IRS Instructions for Form 6765 (updated February 6, 2026), if a taxpayer does not make the IRC Section 280C(c) reduced credit election on Item A of an original timely filed return, domestic research or experimental expenditures under Section 174A otherwise taken into account as a deduction or charged to a capital account must be reduced by the full amount of the Section 41 research credit. Crucially, the OBBBA retained the mandatory 15-year capitalization and amortization regime under IRC Section 174 for all research or experimental expenditures attributable to foreign research (reported via an attached statement on Line 43 of Form 4562). In addition, 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(4)(F) continues to exclude any research conducted outside the United States, the Commonwealth of Puerto Rico, or any possession of the United States from qualifying for the Section 41 tax credit.

Strategic Analysis for Outsourced Engineering: The post-OBBBA regime creates an extraordinary tax-planning asymmetry when selecting third-party engineering or software development contractors. If a United States corporation pays $1,000,000 under a non-contingent research contract to a domestic engineering firm performing qualified research physically within the United States, the corporation immediately deducts $1,000,000 in Year 1 under IRC Section 174A(a) (subject to the IRC Section 280C(c) adjustment) and includes $650,000 (65 percent of $1,000,000) as a contract research QRE under 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(3)(A). Conversely, if that same corporation pays $1,000,000 to an offshore contractor performing the engineering work outside the United States, the corporation receives $0 in Section 41 QREs and can deduct only $33,333.33 (3.3333 percent under the midpoint convention) in Year 1 under IRC Section 174, deferring the remaining $966,666.67 in tax deductions across the subsequent 15 calendar years.
6. IRS Compliance, Refund Substantiation, and the Overhaul of Form 6765
Refund Claim Specificity: CCA 20214101F and the June 2024 / January 2026 Updates

To curb unsubstantiated research credit claims submitted on amended returns, the IRS Office of Chief Counsel issued Field Advice Memorandum Number 20214101F (released October 15, 2021), interpreting the regulatory specificity requirement of 26 CFR § 301.6402-2(b)(1).

First, under the original five-item standard of CCA 20214101F, the fifth required item was to provide total qualified employee wage expenses, total qualified supply expenses, and total qualified contract research expenses for the claim year—which both CCA 20214101F and LB&I-04-0125-0001 explicitly confirm is satisfied by properly completing Form 6765 (rather than requiring component-by-component QRE dollar breakdowns in the initial refund claim narrative itself, a requirement that was introduced separately for post-2025 returns via Section G of revised Form 6765).

Second, effective for research credit refund claims postmarked on or after June 18, 2024, the IRS officially waived the requirement for taxpayers to submit (a) the names of the individuals who performed each research activity and (b) the information each individual sought to discover at the time the initial refund claim is filed (though examiners may still request both items if the claim is selected for audit examination). Consequently, for refund claims postmarked on or after June 18, 2024, satisfying Treasury Regulation § 301.6402-2(b)(1) requires three mandatory items accompanied by a written declaration signed under penalties of perjury:

items: Business Components: Identify all business components (as defined in IRC § 41(d)(2)(B)) that form the factual basis of the research credit claim for the claim year.

Research Activities: Describe all research activities performed by business component, detailing what the taxpayer did and how they did it (language merely restating Code or regulatory requirements is insufficient).

Qualified Expense Totals: Provide the total qualified employee wage expenses, total supply expenses, and total contract research expenses for the claim year (fulfilled by properly completing Form 6765).

body.text: Third, while the IRS provided a transition period for claims filed from January 10, 2022, through January 10, 2026—under which taxpayers submitting a deficient claim were issued Letter 6428 (Claim for Credit for Increasing Research Credit Activities - Additional Information Required) and granted 45 days to perfect the claim—that transition period expired on January 10, 2026. Under LB&I-04-0125-0001, all research credit refund claims filed on or after January 11, 2026, are subject to strict enforcement under IRC Section 6511(a) with no opportunity to perfect: if a post-transition refund claim lacks any of the three mandatory items or a proper perjury declaration, the IRS issues Letter 6430 (No Consideration, Section 41 Claim) directly following Territory Manager/PSP Section Chief and IRS Counsel concurrence, rejecting the claim without audit consideration.
The Overhaul of Form 6765: Section F and Section G Mechanics

In tandem with its administrative refund-claim enforcement, the IRS substantially redesigned Form 6765 (Credit for Increasing Research Activities, Rev. December 2024 / Rev. December 2025; Instructions updated February 6, 2026).

According to the official IRS Instructions for Form 6765 (updated February 6, 2026), Section G (Business Component Information) is optional for all filers for tax years beginning before 2026 (meaning it is optional for both the 2024 and 2025 tax years) and becomes mandatory only for tax years beginning after 2025 (i.e., tax year 2026 and forward), subject to explicit statutory and small-taxpayer exemptions.

At the top of revised Form 6765, taxpayers make the IRC Section 280C reduced credit election on an original timely filed return in Item A and indicate whether they are a member of a controlled group or business under common control in Item B. Non-exempt taxpayers must complete Section G (Columns 49–56) first before carrying totals to Section F (Qualified Research Expenses Summary, Lines 42–48). In Section F, taxpayers itemize current-year QREs across specific lines (reporting only the individual member's QREs if filing a separate return within a controlled group). Specifically, Line 42 reports total qualified in-house employee wages for qualified services across all business components (carried from Column 53 of Section G, if completed, excluding any wages used in figuring the work opportunity credit under IRC § 51(a)); Line 43 reports total qualified supplies (carried from Column 54 of Section G); and Line 44 reports amounts paid or incurred for the rental or lease of off-premises computers used in qualified research where the taxpayer is not the operator or primary user, reduced by any amount received or accrued for the right to use substantially identical property (carried from Column 55 of Section G). Line 45 reports Contract Research Expenses—comprising 75 percent of qualified research consortium payments under § 41(b)(3)(C) and 65 percent of standard third-party contract research payments under § 41(b)(3)(A) (excluding basic research payments reported on Line 46), carried from Column 56 of Section G—while Line 46 reports applicable corporate basic research payments and 100 percent of eligible energy research payments made to eligible small businesses, universities, or federal laboratories under § 41(b)(3)(D), and Line 48 sums Total Qualified Research Expenses, which is then carried to Line 5 (Regular Credit) or Line 20 (Alternative Simplified Credit).

For tax years beginning after 2025, completing Section G is mandatory unless the taxpayer qualifies for one of two exemptions: (1) the taxpayer is a Qualified Small Business (QSB) under IRC § 41(h)(3) electing the reduced payroll tax credit; or (2) the taxpayer's controlled-group total QREs on Line 48 are $1.5 million or less, its average annual gross receipts for the prior 3 tax years under IRC § 448(c)(3) are $50 million or less, and the research credit is claimed on an original timely filed return. Filers required to complete Section G must follow the "80% / Top 50" reporting protocol: listing business components in descending order of total QREs (evaluated at the controlled-group level) and completing Columns 49(a)–(f) (including software classifications such as internal-use software subject to the high-threshold-of-innovation test under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(c)(6) or dual-function software) and Columns 50–56 (allocating direct wages, supervision wages, support wages, supplies, computer leasing, and Column 56 contract research expenses to each discrete business component) until they have reported at least 80 percent of total QREs or a maximum of 50 business components. Any remaining QREs beyond the top 50 components are aggregated on a single summary line labeled "Aggregate Business Components" in Column 49(c).
Federal Credit Calculation Methods: Regular Credit (RRC) vs. Alternative Simplified Credit (ASC)

Once total QREs (including Line 45 contract research expenses) are determined on Line 48 of Form 6765, the taxpayer computes its Section 41 credit under one of two mutually exclusive statutory methods. Under the Regular Research Credit (26 U.S.C. § 41(a)(1) & § 41(c)(1)–(3)), the credit equals 20 percent of the excess of current-year QREs over the statutory base amount. The base amount is the product of the taxpayer's fixed-base percentage multiplied by the taxpayer's average annual gross receipts (reduced by returns and allowances under § 41(c)(6)) for the 4 taxable years preceding the credit year. For established firms that had both QREs and gross receipts in at least three taxable years between January 1, 1984, and December 31, 1988, the fixed-base percentage is the ratio of aggregate QREs to aggregate gross receipts for those 1984–1988 years (26 U.S.C. § 41(c)(3)(A)). For "start-up companies" (firms whose first taxable year with both gross receipts and QREs began after December 31, 1983, or that had fewer than three such years in 1984–1988), 26 U.S.C. § 41(c)(3)(B) sets the fixed-base percentage at 3 percent for each of the taxpayer's first 5 taxable years beginning after December 31, 1993, with QREs, followed by a 5-year phase-in transition across years 6 through 10 (1/6 of the years 4–5 ratio in year 6; 1/3 of years 5–6 in year 7; 1/2 of years 5–7 in year 8; 2/3 of years 5–8 in year 9; 5/6 of years 5–9 in year 10; and the ratio from any 5 years selected by the taxpayer from years 5–10 thereafter). Under 26 U.S.C. § 41(c)(3)(C)–(D), the fixed-base percentage is rounded to the nearest 1/100th of 1 percent and cannot exceed a maximum cap of 16 percent. Furthermore, under 26 U.S.C. § 41(c)(2), the minimum base amount cannot be less than 50 percent of current-year QREs, and under 26 U.S.C. § 41(c)(5)(A) (the consistency rule), base-period QREs must be determined on a basis consistent with current-year QREs.

Alternatively, under the Alternative Simplified Credit (26 U.S.C. § 41(c)(4)), at the election of the taxpayer (which applies to the election year and all succeeding taxable years unless revoked with the consent of the Secretary under § 41(c)(4)(C)), the credit equals 14 percent of so much of the current-year QREs as exceeds 50 percent of the average QREs for the 3 preceding taxable years. Under 26 U.S.C. § 41(c)(4)(B), if the taxpayer had no QREs in any one of the 3 preceding taxable years, the ASC credit rate is reduced to 6 percent of current-year QREs.
7. State R&D Tax Credit Frameworks and Treatment of Contract Research

Multistate corporations claiming contract research expenses under IRC Section 41(b)(3) must navigate sharp statutory divergences across state tax regimes. While most states conform to IRC Section 41 as a foundational starting point, they impose strict in-state geographic sourcing rules, modified base-period and credit rate formulas, statewide annual program caps, or outright exclusions of third-party contract research.
California (Cal. Rev. & Tax. Code § 23609 and § 17052.12)

California provides a permanent, non-refundable Research Credit codified under California Revenue and Taxation Code (R&TC) § 23609 (for corporations under the Corporation Tax Law) and R&TC § 17052.12 (for personal income tax filers and pass-through entities under the Personal Income Tax Law), claimed on Form FTB 3523 (Research Credit). Unlike federal tax law during the 2022–2024 TCJA window, California never conformed to the TCJA Section 174 mandatory capitalization rules, permitting uninterrupted immediate state-level deductibility of R&D expenditures. Unused California R&D tax credits carry forward indefinitely until exhausted; however, under California unitary combined reporting rules, R&D credits cannot be pooled or shared across sibling members of a combined reporting group and must be utilized solely against the tax liability of the specific corporate entity that incurred the California QREs.
1. The Strict In-State Geographic Nexus Requirement

Under R&TC § 23609(c)(2) and the Instructions for Form FTB 3523, California conforms to the federal IRC Section 41(b)(3) contract research inclusion rates—allowing 65 percent of standard contract research expenses (as well as 65 percent of the portion of corporate basic research payments that does not exceed the base period amount) and 75 percent of payments made to nonprofit qualified research consortia under IRC § 501(c)(3) or § 501(c)(6)—but enforces a strict geographic boundary: only qualified research physically conducted in California qualifies. If a California corporation engages an out-of-state engineering contractor that performs the research in Texas or Massachusetts, 0 percent of that invoice qualifies for the California credit. Where a third-party vendor performs research partially inside California and partially outside California, the taxpayer must substantiate a reasonable allocation and may claim 65 percent of only the specific portion of the contract research physically performed within California.
2. California Administrative and Judicial Precedents

First, California Franchise Tax Board (FTB) Legal Ruling 2021-01 (issued October 25, 2021) is titled Unity of Apportioning Pass-through Entities and addresses when pass-through entity holding companies are unitary with operating pass-through entities—it does not address the R&D tax credit at all. Second, the regulatory language declaring that "a determination of eligibility for the federal credit is not binding on the determination of eligibility for the state credit" and requiring that "taxpayers prove entitlement to the credit by clear and convincing evidence, with proof of qualified research expenses supported by contemporaneous business records" was actually promulgated by the Texas Comptroller of Public Accounts in its October 2021 amendments to 34 TAC § 3.599 (which was summarized right next to California Legal Ruling 2021-01 in the November 2021 Plante Moran newsletter). In California, while an IRS audit acceptance is likewise not legally binding on the FTB's independent audit authority (as demonstrated in Appeal of Pacific Coast Building Products, Inc., where the FTB disallowed 100 percent of claimed California R&D credits for fiscal years ended 1999–2004 despite the IRS accepting the taxpayer's FYE 2005–2006 credits with no change), California's "clear and convincing evidence" burden in the cited case law applies to a party seeking an alternative apportionment formula under R&TC § 25137.
Primary judicial and administrative records establish the exact forum and legal holding of each precedent.

In Appeal of Electronic Data Systems Corporation & Subsidiaries, 2023-OTA-540 (Cal. Office of Tax Appeals, June 14, 2023, Nonprecedential), the OTA held: (1) for tax years 2003 and 2004, the OTA lacked jurisdiction over the taxpayer's regular research credit claim because the taxpayer's 2012 administrative refund claim explicitly elected and computed only the Alternative Incremental Credit (AIC) under IRC § 41(c)(4), failing to provide the FTB with actual notice or base-period data for a regular research credit claim (and thus failing to exhaust administrative remedies); and (2) for tax years 2005 through 2008, the taxpayer failed to substantiate its California gross receipts calculation under R&TC § 23609(h)(3) (now § 23609(i)). Specifically, the OTA rejected the taxpayer's initial attempt to compute California research gross receipts simply by multiplying total federal net gross receipts by its California Schedule R apportionment percentage, and further held that the taxpayer failed to substantiate its excluded service and non-sale revenue streams to prove the exact amount of gross receipts from sales of property held primarily for sale to customers in the ordinary course of business delivered or shipped to purchasers in California. (The OTA also noted FTB Legal Division Guidance 2012-03-01, issued March 1, 2012, which clarified that a taxpayer with California QREs but zero California gross receipts under R&TC § 23609(h)(3) may still claim the regular research credit subject to the 50 percent minimum base floor).

Conversely, Appeal of Pacific Coast Building Products, Inc., et al., Case No. 514183 (Cal. State Board of Equalization [BOE], Summary Decision, oral hearings Sept. 12, 2012 & Oct. 29, 2013, Nonprecedential), was decided by the California State Board of Equalization (BOE) (the constitutional predecessor tribunal to the OTA prior to 2018), adjudicating whether 64 manufacturing projects across California facilities satisfied the IRC § 41(d) process of experimentation test, QRE substantiation, and fixed-base percentage consistency rules for fiscal years ended March 31, 1999, through March 31, 2004. Finally, the landmark 2006 decision in Microsoft Corp. v. Franchise Tax Board, 39 Cal. 4th 750 (Cal. 2006) (see also Microsoft Corp. v. FTB, 212 Cal. App. 4th 78 (2012)), on gross receipts distortion was decided by the California Supreme Court (not the OTA), holding that while gross proceeds from marketable treasury securities redemptions constituted gross receipts under the general UDITPA sales factor, the FTB established by clear and convincing evidence under R&TC § 25137 that including full redemption principal distorted California business activity (and FTB Legal Ruling 2019-01 expressly clarifies that R&TC § 25137 applies solely to UDITPA allocation and apportionment, not to tax credit base calculations). (A subsequent February 2024 OTA decision in Appeal of Microsoft Corp. & Subsidiaries, OTA Case No. 21037336, addressed foreign dividend repatriation under water's-edge apportionment, not R&TC § 23609).
3. California Credit Methodologies: RRC, the 2025 Repeal of the AIC/AIRC, and SB 711's New ASC

Under R&TC § 23609 and the 2025 Instructions for Form FTB 3523, the California Regular Research Credit (RRC) equals 15 percent of current-year California QREs exceeding the California base period amount (calculated by multiplying the fixed-base percentage—capped at 16 percent—by the average annual California gross receipts from sales of property held primarily for sale to customers in the ordinary course of business delivered or shipped to a purchaser within California over the 4 preceding taxable years, subject to the 50 percent minimum base floor). In addition, corporations (excluding S corporations) may claim an additional 24 percent credit on basic research payments made to qualified universities and scientific research organizations in excess of the base period amount.

First, for taxable years beginning on or after January 1, 2025, the California Alternative Incremental Credit (AIC / AIRC)—which previously applied tiered rates of 1.49 percent, 1.98 percent, and 2.48 percent against thresholds of the prior 4 years' average California gross receipts (not 3 years) for tax years through 2024—has been repealed and is no longer available for California tax purposes. Taxpayers who previously elected the AIC do not automatically default to either the regular credit or the ASC; they must affirmatively elect either the Regular Research Credit or the new California ASC on a timely filed original return using Form FTB 3523.

Second, for taxable years beginning on or after January 1, 2025, California conforms (with rate modifications) to the federal ASC framework under IRC § 41(c)(4). Under the new California ASC, the credit equals 3 percent (modifying the federal 14 percent rate in § 41(c)(4)(A)) of current-year California QREs that exceed 50 percent of the average California QREs for the 3 preceding taxable years, or 1.3 percent (modifying the federal 6 percent rate in § 41(c)(4)(B)(ii)) of current-year California QREs if the taxpayer had no California QREs in any one of the 3 preceding taxable years. Once made on a timely filed original return, the ASC election applies to that taxable year and all subsequent years unless the FTB grants consent to revoke, and the FTB explicitly advises taxpayers with zero California gross receipts to elect the ASC.
Comparative Analysis of Alternative State Frameworks
1. New York Life Sciences R&D Tax Credit (NY Tax Law § 43 & § 210-B)

Administered jointly by Empire State Development (ESD) and the New York State Department of Taxation and Finance under New York Tax Law § 43 and § 210-B (and regulated under 5 NYCRR § 260-43), the New York State Life Sciences Research and Development Tax Credit Program provides a fully refundable tax credit to certified new life sciences businesses. The credit equals 20 percent of qualified research expenses incurred within New York State for certified companies employing fewer than 10 employees (determined by averaging headcount across March 31, June 30, September 30, and December 31) and 15 percent for certified companies employing 10 or more employees. The credit is capped at $500,000 per year per taxpayer for a maximum of 3 consecutive years (yielding a $1.5 million lifetime ceiling per company), allocated out of a statewide aggregate cap of $10 million per year. In a stark statutory departure from IRC Section 41(b)(3), New York explicitly excludes 100 percent of contract research expenses (0 percent inclusion) from the Life Sciences R&D credit base, restricting eligible New York QREs strictly to in-house employee wages, direct supplies, and computer usage costs physically incurred within New York State.
2. Texas R&D Franchise Tax Credit (Tex. Tax Code Ch. 171, Subchapter T, Enacted by SB 2206)

Effective January 1, 2026, Texas Senate Bill 2206 (89th Legislature, Regular Session) repealed both the former Subchapter M franchise tax credit and the R&D sales and use tax exemption under Texas Tax Code § 151.3182 (which the legislature found inefficient to administer), replacing both with the enhanced, permanent Subchapter T Franchise Tax Credit (Tex. Tax Code §§ 171.9201–171.9210). (Under transition rules, a taxable entity or combined group member that received a sales tax exemption under § 151.3182 during the period on which a 2026 or 2027 report is based is prohibited from claiming the Subchapter T credit for that period).

In the actual statutory text of Texas Tax Code § 171.9204(a)–(d) and Texas Comptroller Form 05-917 (Instructions for Subchapter T Research and Development Activities Refundable Credit Forms 05-183 and 05-184), the 8.722 percent rate is the standard Subchapter T credit rate, which is already calculated using an ASC-style rolling base equal to 50 percent of the average qualified research expenses incurred in Texas (QRET) during the 3 preceding tax periods. The higher 10.903 percent rate is not an "alternative simplified method"; rather, under § 171.9204(b), 10.903 percent applies when the taxable entity contracts with one or more public or private institutions of higher education for the performance of qualified research in Texas and incurs QRET under that contract during the report period. Furthermore, if the taxable entity had zero QRET in one or more of the 3 preceding tax periods, the credit rate is 4.361 percent of current-period QRET (or 5.451 percent of current-period QRET if contracting with a public or private institution of higher education).

Moreover, per Form 05-917, QRETs are defined directly as expenses reported on Line 48 of IRS Form 6765 limited strictly to research conducted in Texas (thus conforming to the 65 percent and 75 percent contract research inclusion rules of IRC § 41(b)(3)), and a taxpayer that did not report federal QREs on Line 48 of IRS Form 6765 (a copy of which must be attached) is ineligible for the Texas credit. For tax-owing entities (claiming the credit on Forms 05-181 and 05-182 with Form 05-158), the credit is capped annually at 50 percent of franchise tax due with a 20-year carryforward (§§ 171.9207–171.9208). Crucially, however, under Texas Tax Code § 171.9205 (claimed via Form 05-183 and Form 05-184 on or before November 15), the credit is 100 percent refundable (exempt from the 50 percent limitation) for any taxable entity (other than an EZ computation filer) that owes zero franchise tax because (a) its annualized total revenue is at or below the No Tax Due Threshold ($2.65 million in 2026), (b) its computed franchise tax is less than $1,000, or (c) it is a qualified new veteran-owned business.
3. Pennsylvania, Maryland, South Carolina, and Illinois

In Pennsylvania (72 P.S. §§ 8701-B to 8712-B, Tax Reform Code of 1971, Article XVII-B), Section 1702-B (72 P.S. § 8702-B) adopts the federal IRC § 41(b) definition of QREs—including the 65 percent contract research inclusion rate for qualified research physically conducted in Pennsylvania. Under Section 1709-B(a) (72 P.S. § 8709-B(a)), aggregate statewide R&D tax credits approved by the Pennsylvania Department of Revenue are capped at $60,000,000 ($60 million) per fiscal year (with $12,000,000 set aside exclusively for small businesses), requiring pro-rata allocation across approved applicants whenever statewide claims exceed the annual cap.

Verification against the Maryland Department of Legislative Services (Issue Papers: 2025 Legislative Session — Evaluation of the Research and Development Tax Credit, December 2024) confirms that Chapter 114 of the 2021 Maryland Laws repealed the 3 percent Basic R&D Tax Credit (effective beginning in tax year 2020) and dedicated the entire $12.0 million annual statewide cap solely to the 10 percent Growth R&D Tax Credit for Maryland QREs (including 65 percent of Maryland contract research expenses) exceeding the Maryland Base Amount (with $3.5 million of the $12.0 million reserved annually for refundable credits for qualified small businesses, and the statutory program scheduled to sunset on June 30, 2027).

In South Carolina (S.C. Code Ann. § 12-6-3415, Form SC SCH.TC-18), the state provides a non-refundable credit equal to 5 percent of qualified research expenses incurred within South Carolina, adopting the federal IRC § 41 QRE definitions wholesale (including the 65 percent contract research inclusion under § 41(b)(3) and the funded research exclusion under § 41(d)(4)(H)), capped annually at 50 percent of remaining tax liability after all other credits with a 10-year carryforward. Similarly, in Illinois (35 ILCS 5/201(k) & 86 Ill. Adm. Code 100.2160, Schedule 1299-D), the state provides a non-refundable credit equal to 6.5 percent of qualifying expenditures for increasing research activities physically conducted in Illinois over the base period amount (defined as the average Illinois QREs for the 3 preceding taxable years), conforming to IRC § 41(b) and § 41(d) (including 65 percent of Illinois contract research expenses) with a 5-year carryforward.

body.text: 8. Hypothetical Worked Example: Multijurisdictional Contract Research Analysis (2026 Tax Year)
Hypothetical Fact Pattern

Assume TechCorp, a surgical robotics manufacturer headquartered in San Jose, California, conducts a major R&D program during calendar tax year 2026 to develop a next-generation autonomous surgical robot (a single new business component satisfying the four-part test of IRC § 41(d)(1)). Prior to the performance of any research, TechCorp executes formal written agreements with three unrelated third-party contractors totaling $1,100,000 in 2026 payments, all for engineering services performed entirely during calendar year 2026.

First, under a $500,000 Cost-Plus-Fixed-Fee (CPFF) Agreement with Contractor X (San Francisco, California), Contractor X is engaged to develop a proprietary machine-learning kinematics algorithm in San Francisco, California. Under the CPFF contract, TechCorp is contractually obligated to reimburse Contractor X's incurred engineering labor and direct costs plus a fixed fee regardless of whether the algorithm achieves its target latency specifications, and TechCorp receives exclusive intellectual property rights to the research results.

Second, under a $400,000 Firm-Fixed-Price (FFP) Agreement with Contractor Y (Austin, Texas), Contractor Y is engaged to engineer and prototype a lightweight titanium chassis in Austin, Texas. Under the FFP contract, payment of the $400,000 is strictly contingent upon Contractor Y delivering a prototype chassis that passes formal structural stress-testing acceptance protocols; if the design fails stress testing, Contractor Y must re-engineer and remedy the chassis at its own expense or forfeit payment. While TechCorp receives exclusive commercial ownership of the physical chassis blueprints, the contract does not prohibit Contractor Y from using the underlying metallurgical research methods and know-how in its own business without paying TechCorp.

Third, under a $200,000 Time-and-Materials (T&M) Agreement with Contractor Z (London, United Kingdom), Contractor Z is engaged to perform experimental secondary user-interface software development in London, United Kingdom. TechCorp pays Contractor Z on an hourly time-and-materials basis regardless of technical success and retains all intellectual property rights.
Step-by-Step Recomputed Tax Analysis
1. Federal Contract Research QRE (26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(3)(A)) and Section 174 / 174A Deduction Analysis

For Contractor X ($500,000 CPFF, San Francisco, CA), TechCorp entered into the agreement prior to performance, retains exclusive rights to the research results ("on behalf of" under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(e)(3)), and must reimburse Contractor X's incurred costs plus a fixed fee regardless of technical outcome (Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(e)(2)(iii)), meaning TechCorp bears the financial risk of failure. Because the research is performed physically within the United States (IRC § 41(d)(4)(F)), applying the 65 percent standard inclusion rate under 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(3)(A) yields a Federal Contract QRE of $325,000 ($500,000 × 65% = $325,000). Conversely, because the research is fully "funded" by TechCorp under IRC § 41(d)(4)(H) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d) (and Contractor X retains no substantial rights), Contractor X may claim $0 of its internal costs on this project. Under IRC Section 174A(a) (enacted by the OBBBA, P.L. 119-21), because the expenditure is for domestic research incurred in tax year 2026 (after December 31, 2024), TechCorp may immediately deduct 100 percent ($500,000) in 2026 (subject to the IRC Section 280C(c) adjustment).

For Contractor Y ($400,000 Contingent FFP, Austin, TX), because payment of the $400,000 is strictly contingent upon Contractor Y delivering a prototype chassis that passes stress-testing acceptance protocols, the payment is treated as paid for the product or result rather than the performance of research under Treasury Regulation § 1.41-2(e)(2)(iii) and Fairchild Industries. Consequently, TechCorp's eligible contract research QRE is $0 ($400,000 × 0% = $0). Conversely, because the research is not funded by TechCorp and Contractor Y retains non-exclusive substantial rights to use its underlying metallurgical know-how under Populous Holdings and Lockheed Martin, Contractor Y may claim 100 percent of its own eligible in-house employee wages and supplies in Austin for both the Federal IRC § 41 credit and the Texas Subchapter T credit.

For Contractor Z ($200,000 T&M, London, UK), although TechCorp bears the financial risk of failure under the T&M contract, the research is physically conducted outside the United States (in the United Kingdom) and is therefore 100 percent excluded from the research credit under 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(4)(F), yielding a Federal QRE of $0 ($200,000 × 0% = $0). Furthermore, under IRC Section 174 (retained for foreign research by the OBBBA, P.L. 119-21), TechCorp must charge the $200,000 foreign research expenditure to a capital account and amortize it ratably over 15 years beginning with the midpoint of 2026. This limits TechCorp's Year 1 (2026) amortization deduction to $6,666.67 ($200,000 × (1 / 15) × 0.5 = $6,666.67, or 3.3333 percent), followed by $13,333.33 per year ($200,000 / 15, or 6.6667 percent per year) in Years 2 through 15 (2027–2040), and a final midpoint deduction of $6,666.67 in Year 16 (2041), leaving $193,333.33 unamortized at the end of 2026.

Summing all three contractors, TechCorp's Total Federal Contract QREs (reported on Form 6765, Section G Column 56 and Section F Line 45) equal $325,000 ($325,000 + $0 + $0 = $325,000), and TechCorp's Total Year 1 R&E Deduction (across Contractors X and Z) equals $506,666.67 ($500,000 + $6,666.67).
2. State QRE Analysis (California, Texas, and New York)

Under California (R&TC § 23609, Form FTB 3523), Contractor X's research is funded by TechCorp and physically performed in San Francisco, California, so 65 percent qualifies, yielding $325,000 ($500,000 × 65% = $325,000). Contractor Y is disqualified from TechCorp's California claim on two independent legal grounds—failing the financial risk test (contingent FFP) and failing the California in-state geographic requirement (physically performed in Austin, Texas)—yielding $0 in California QREs. Contractor Z fails the California geographic requirement (performed in London, UK), yielding $0. Thus, TechCorp's Total California Contract QREs equal $325,000.

Under Texas (Tex. Tax Code Ch. 171, Subchapter T, Form 05-917), although Contractor Y performed the chassis research in Austin, Texas, TechCorp cannot include Contractor Y's $400,000 fee on Line 48 of its federal Form 6765 because the FFP contract was contingent on success ($0 federal QRE), yielding $0 in Texas QREs (QRET) for TechCorp. (However, Contractor Y itself can include 100 percent of its eligible Austin employee wages and supplies on its own federal Form 6765 Line 48 and claim the 8.722 percent Texas Subchapter T credit on its excess QRET over 50 percent of its prior 3-year average QRET).

Under the New York Life Sciences R&D Tax Credit (NY Tax Law § 43), even if TechCorp were a certified life sciences company and had engaged a contractor inside New York State, 100 percent of contract research expenses are statutorily excluded under New York's program, yielding $0 in New York QREs across all three contractors.
